MODULES.title: What AI Actually Is
MODULES.tag: LLMs demystified: a text-prediction machine, not a mind
MODULES.why: Almost everything people call "AI" today runs on the same kind of engine: a large language model. If you understand what that engine really does, and the few things it can't do, you'll stop being surprised by it. You'll know when to trust it, when to double-check it, and why it behaves the way it does. Every other lesson in this course builds on this one idea.
MODULES.mental: A large language model is a text-prediction machine. You give it some text, and it guesses the most likely next chunk of text, over and over, until it has written a full answer. That's the whole trick. It is not looking anything up, it has no memory of you, and it isn't "thinking" the way a person does. Once you picture it as a very, very well-read autocomplete, the rest of AI stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like a tool with rules.
concepts: LLM (large language model)

The engine behind ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. It's a program trained on an enormous amount of text, and its one job is to predict what text comes next. That simple skill, done extremely well, is enough to write, summarize, answer questions, and even code.
Predicting the next word

When you ask the model something, it builds its answer one piece at a time, each time guessing the most likely next piece based on everything so far. Nothing is written in advance, the whole answer is assembled on the spot.
Training
Before you ever use it, the model was shown a huge amount of text and slowly tuned to get better at predicting it. This happened once, in advance. Using the model later doesn't teach it anything new.
It sounds confident either way
Because the model's goal is to produce text that reads well, it phrases a wrong answer just as smoothly as a right one. Confidence in the wording tells you nothing about whether it's correct.
Not a search engine

A search engine finds existing pages and shows them to you. A language model doesn't look anything up by default, it generates new text from patterns it learned. That's why it can be creative, and also why it can make things up.
Same engine, many products

ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all chat products built on top of large language models. The chat window, the memory features, the ability to see images, those are extras added around the core text-prediction engine.
mistakes: Thinking the model "knows" things the way a database does, it's predicting likely text, not retrieving stored facts
Trusting an answer because it sounds confident, fluent wording and correctness are unrelated
Expecting it to remember a past conversation on its own, by default each chat starts fresh
Assuming it searched the web, unless a product explicitly adds that, it didn't
Treating it as a calculator for exact math or precise quotes, it predicts plausible text, which isn't the same as being exact
flags: "The AI told me, so it must be right", confidence isn't evidence; verify anything that matters
"It made up a fact / a fake quote / a broken link", that's the prediction engine filling a gap, not a glitch you can fully turn off
"It forgot what I said earlier", you likely hit the limits of its short-term memory, covered in the context lesson
"It gave me a different answer the second time", normal, the model makes fresh guesses each time
ask: Is this a question where being wrong would cost me, and if so, how will I check the answer?
Am I expecting it to recall something, or to generate something? (It's much better at generating.)
Could this need fresh or private information the model was never trained on?
Would a real source (a search, a document, a person) be a better fit than a confident guess?

MODULES.title: Tokens & How Models Read Text
MODULES.tag: The model doesn't read words, it reads tokens, and that explains a lot
MODULES.why: You're billed in tokens, you run out of room in tokens, and a few of the model's weirdest quirks (bad spelling tricks, shaky math, trouble counting letters) come straight from tokens. You don't need to count them by hand, but once you know what a token is, three confusing things about AI suddenly make sense: why it costs what it costs, why it sometimes forgets, and why it stumbles on tasks that look easy.
MODULES.mental: Before the model can predict the next chunk of text, it has to chop your text into pieces. Those pieces are called tokens. A token is usually a short run of characters, often about three-quarters of a word, so common words are one token, and longer or unusual words get split into several. The model never sees letters or whole words the way you do, it sees a stream of tokens. Picture it reading text in puzzle pieces rather than letters: that one image explains the cost, the limits, and the quirks you'll meet for the rest of this course.
concepts: Token

The small chunk of text a model actually reads and writes. Often a common word, a word-piece, a space, or a punctuation mark. As a rough rule of thumb, one token is about four characters of English, or roughly three-quarters of a word.
Tokenizing
The step where your text is sliced into tokens before the model sees it. It happens automatically, every time, for both what you send in and what the model writes back.
Why splitting helps

There are too many possible words (and typos, and names) to give each its own slot. Breaking text into a few thousand reusable pieces lets the model handle any text, even words it never saw, by spelling them out of smaller pieces.
Tokens, not words, are the unit

Length limits and pricing are measured in tokens, not words or characters. A long word can be several tokens, and a space or comma can be its own token, so token counts rarely match word counts exactly.
Input tokens and output tokens
Everything you send (your question, plus any text you paste in) is input tokens. Everything the model writes back is output tokens. Both count, and longer of either means slower and more expensive.
Where the quirks come from

Because the model sees tokens, not letters, tasks that depend on individual characters get hard: counting the letters in a word, reversing it, or precise spelling. It's not that the model is dumb here, it just isn't looking at letters.
mistakes: Assuming one word equals one token, short common words are one token, but longer or rarer words split into several, so counts don't line up
Forgetting that the text you paste in counts too, a long document you attach can use far more tokens than your actual question
Being surprised the model miscounts letters or botches a word-reversal, it reads tokens, not letters, so character-level tasks are genuinely its weak spot
Thinking only your input is billed, the answer the model writes (output tokens) costs too, and is often the bigger half
Expecting other languages to cost the same, text in many non-English languages splits into more tokens, so the same meaning can cost more
flags: "Why did this short chat cost so much?", you probably pasted in a long document; that input is tokens too
"It can't tell me how many r's are in a word", classic token blind spot, it isn't seeing the letters
"It cut off mid-answer", you likely hit a length limit measured in tokens, covered next lesson on the context window
"The same request is pricier in my language", some languages tokenize into more pieces, so they cost more for the same content
ask: Am I about to paste in a lot of text? If so, that's a lot of tokens, do I really need all of it?
Is this a letter-by-letter task (counting characters, exact spelling, reversing a word)? If so, the model may struggle, and a simple tool would be more reliable.
Could I get the same result with a shorter prompt or a shorter requested answer, to save time and cost?
If cost matters, have I checked roughly how many tokens my typical request uses?

MODULES.title: The Context Window
MODULES.tag: The model's short-term memory, and why it's smaller than you think
MODULES.why: This one idea explains the single most common frustration people have with AI: "why did it forget what I just told it?" The model can only look at a limited amount of text at once, called the context window. Everything it knows in the moment, your question, the conversation so far, any file you pasted, has to fit inside that window. Understand the window and you'll know why long chats drift, why pasting a giant document can backfire, and how to keep the model on track.
MODULES.mental: The model has no memory of its own between messages. Each time you hit send, it's handed one big block of text, the conversation so far plus your new message, and it reads only that. The size limit on that block is the context window. Think of it as the model's desk, not its filing cabinet: only what's on the desk right now can be used, and the desk has an edge. When the conversation grows past that edge, the oldest things slide off and are simply gone. The model isn't choosing to forget, it literally never sees what fell off the desk.
concepts: Context window

The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, the model can look at in one go. It has to hold everything at once: the conversation history, your current message, any pasted files, and the answer being written.
It's the model's working memory
Whatever is in the window is what the model 'knows' in this moment. It doesn't remember earlier chats, and within a chat it only has what still fits in the window right now.
Falling off the edge
When a conversation gets longer than the window, the earliest messages stop being included. The model can't refer back to them because, from its point of view, they're no longer there.
Bigger windows, real limits
Modern models have large windows (often enough for many pages, sometimes a whole book), but the limit is still real, still measured in tokens, and using a big window is slower and costs more.
More text isn't always better

Stuffing the window with everything you have can actually hurt, the important detail gets buried in noise and the model may latch onto the wrong thing. A focused, relevant context usually beats a huge one.
You control the window
You decide what goes in: a tight question with just the needed details, or a long ramble with a pasted novel. Curating what the model sees is the most practical skill in this whole course.
mistakes: Assuming the model remembers everything you've ever said to it, within a chat it only has what still fits the window, and across chats it remembers nothing by default
Pasting in a huge document and expecting laser-accurate recall, the more you cram in, the easier it is for the key detail to get lost
Blaming the model for 'forgetting' early parts of a very long conversation, those parts likely fell off the edge of the window
Thinking a bigger context window is always better, it costs more, runs slower, and can dilute the important bits
Burying the actual question at the top of a wall of text, the model does best when the ask is clear and the context around it is relevant
flags: "It forgot a detail I gave it ten messages ago", that detail probably slid off the edge of the window; restate it
"It's ignoring most of the long document I pasted", important parts may be buried; give it just the relevant section
"Long chats get worse over time", normal drift as early context drops off; starting a fresh chat with a clean summary often fixes it
"It mixed up two different things I asked about", too much unrelated stuff in the window at once; keep one task per conversation when it matters
ask: Does the model actually have, in this conversation, the detail I'm expecting it to use? If not, I need to include it.
Am I giving it the relevant context, or just a lot of context? Could I trim this down to what matters?
Has this chat gotten really long? Would starting fresh with a short summary work better?
Is my real question easy to spot, or is it buried under everything I pasted?

MODULES.title: Talking to the Model: Prompting Basics
MODULES.tag: The words you give it are the steering wheel, small changes, big differences
MODULES.why: The same model can give you a vague, useless answer or a sharp, exactly-what-you-wanted one, and the only thing that changed was how you asked. That request you type is called a prompt, and learning to write a good one is the highest-leverage skill in this whole course. You don't need clever tricks or secret phrases. You need a few plain habits that get you from "meh" to "that's perfect" far more often.
MODULES.mental: A prompt is just the text you give the model to work with, and the model takes it completely literally, it can't read your mind or see what's on your screen. So think of prompting as briefing a brilliant, eager new assistant on their first day: they're capable and fast, but they know nothing about your situation unless you tell them. The clearer you are about the task, the context, and what a good answer looks like, the better the result. A vague brief gets a vague reply, a specific brief gets a specific one. You're not casting a spell, you're writing a good set of instructions.
concepts: Prompt

The text you send the model, your question or instruction, plus any context or examples you include. It's the entire input the model has to work from, so whatever you leave out, it simply doesn't know.
Be specific about the task

Tell the model exactly what you want it to do. "Write something about dogs" and "Write a friendly three-sentence intro for a dog-walking flyer" produce very different results, because the second one actually says what success looks like.
Give it the context it needs

The model only knows what you tell it in the prompt. Who's the audience, what's the goal, what background matters? Including the relevant context is usually the difference between a generic answer and one that fits your situation.
Say what a good answer looks like
Ask for the format you want: a bulleted list, a short paragraph, a table, a specific tone, a length. The model is happy to oblige, but only if you say so, otherwise it guesses.
Show an example
If you have a sample of the style or format you want, paste it in and say "like this." One good example often teaches the model more than a paragraph of instructions.
Iterate, don't expect perfection first try

Prompting is a conversation. If the first answer is close but not right, tell it what to change ("shorter," "more formal," "focus on the second point"). Refining is normal and usually faster than rewriting from scratch.
mistakes: Being too vague, a one-line request with no context gets a generic answer, the model fills the gaps with guesses
Assuming the model can see what you see, it can't read your screen, your files, or your mind, only the words in the prompt
Not saying what format or length you want, then being annoyed it wrote five paragraphs when you wanted three bullets
Giving up after one mediocre answer instead of refining, the second or third pass is usually where it gets good
Piling on so many instructions at once that the important one gets lost, sometimes it's better to do it in steps
flags: "It gave me something generic and bland", the prompt was probably too vague; add the task, the audience, and the format you want
"It answered a slightly different question than I meant", it took your wording literally; restate the ask more precisely
"It's the right idea but the wrong shape", you likely didn't specify format or length; just ask for the shape you want
"It keeps missing one requirement", too much crammed in one prompt; pull that requirement out and handle it as its own step
ask: Have I actually said what I want, clearly enough that a stranger could follow it?
Does the model have the context it needs, or am I assuming it knows something I never told it?
Did I say what a good answer looks like, the format, length, and tone?
If the first answer is close, what one change would I ask for to make it right?

MODULES.title: How Chat Works
MODULES.tag: There's no "it" remembering you, just the same block of text, re-sent every turn
MODULES.why: Chatting with an AI feels like talking to someone who's following along. But under the hood, there's no "someone" keeping track, the chat is a clever illusion built on top of a model with no memory. Understanding how that illusion actually works clears up a surprising number of confusions: why a new chat starts blank, why "memory" features are a separate add-on, and why the model can suddenly contradict itself. Once you see the mechanism, you'll use chat tools with far less surprise.
MODULES.mental: The model itself is stateless, a fancy word for "it remembers nothing between turns." Each message you send, it sees fresh, with no recollection of the last one. So how does a conversation hold together? The chat app does the remembering for it. Every time you hit send, the app quietly re-sends the entire conversation so far, all of it, your messages and the model's replies, glued together, with your new message tacked on the end. The model reads that whole block, answers, and forgets again. Picture it as a brilliant expert with no memory, handed a complete transcript before every single reply. The continuity you feel isn't in the model, it's in the transcript the app keeps re-handing it.
concepts: Stateless

The model keeps no memory between turns. Each request is handled on its own, as if it were the first thing you'd ever said. Any sense of an ongoing conversation comes from outside the model, not from the model itself.
Conversation history
The running transcript of everything said so far, your messages and the model's replies. The chat app stores this and re-sends the whole thing each turn so the model has the full picture.
The illusion of memory

Because the app re-feeds the entire history every turn, the model appears to remember. It isn't, it's re-reading the transcript each time. Same effect, completely different mechanism, and the difference matters when things go wrong.
A new chat is a blank slate
Start a fresh conversation and the transcript is empty, so the model knows nothing about your previous chats. That's not a bug, it's the default, each chat is its own separate transcript.
"Memory" features are an extra layer

Some products add a real memory feature that saves notes about you and slips them into the transcript automatically. That's a feature built on top of the model, not something the model does on its own, and you can usually see and edit what it stored.
System message (the hidden brief)

Most chat tools quietly add an instruction at the very top of the transcript, before your first word, telling the model how to behave ("You are a helpful assistant"). You don't see it, but it's part of every turn, shaping the tone and rules of the whole chat.
mistakes: Thinking the model is personally remembering you, it's the app re-sending the transcript; the model itself recalls nothing
Expecting a brand-new chat to know about an earlier one, by default each chat is a separate, blank transcript
Assuming a "memory" feature means the model learned something, it just saved a note and slips it into the transcript; the model still didn't change
Being surprised the model contradicts what it said an hour ago in a long chat, if that part fell out of the window, it's no longer in the transcript it sees
Not realizing a hidden system message is shaping every answer, the tool's built-in instructions are part of the conversation too
flags: "It doesn't remember my last chat", expected; each new conversation starts with an empty transcript unless a memory feature is on
"It suddenly forgot what we agreed earlier", in a long chat that part may have dropped out of the window, so it's no longer in the transcript
"The memory feature remembered something weird about me", that's a stored note you can usually view and delete in settings
"It behaves with a personality I didn't ask for", that's often the hidden system message the product added; a different tool will have a different one
ask: Am I expecting this chat to know something from a different conversation? If so, I need to bring it in, it won't carry over by itself.
Is this a fresh chat, or a long one where early details may have dropped off the transcript?
If I'm relying on a memory feature, do I actually know what it has stored about me?
Could a hidden system message be shaping these answers in a way I should account for?

MODULES.title: What Models Get Wrong
MODULES.tag: Hallucination and the knowledge cutoff, the two failure modes you must always expect
MODULES.why: A model that's right ninety percent of the time and confident one hundred percent of the time is genuinely dangerous if you don't know where the ten percent hides. This lesson names the two big, predictable ways models go wrong: they invent things that sound true (hallucination), and they don't know anything recent (the knowledge cutoff). These aren't rare glitches, they're built into how the engine works. Knowing exactly when to expect them is what separates someone who gets burned by AI from someone who uses it safely.
MODULES.mental: Both failures come straight from the one idea you already know: the model predicts likely-sounding text, it doesn't look anything up. So when it doesn't have a real answer, it doesn't stop, it produces the most plausible-sounding text instead, and that invented-but-convincing answer is a hallucination. And because the model was trained once, in the past, its knowledge stops at a certain date, the knowledge cutoff, after which it knows nothing unless a tool feeds it fresh information. Picture a brilliant expert who's been locked in a room since some date last year, and who, rather than ever saying "I don't know," will smoothly make something up. That single image tells you exactly when to be careful: anything recent, and anything where a confident guess would cost you.
concepts: Hallucination

When the model states something false as if it were true, a fake statistic, an invented quote, a citation to a paper that doesn't exist, a made-up feature. It happens because the model fills gaps with plausible text rather than admitting it doesn't know.
Why hallucination can't be fully switched off

It's the same machinery that makes the model useful: always producing likely-sounding text. You can reduce it (better prompts, giving it real sources, asking it to cite), but there's no setting that guarantees it never makes things up.
Knowledge cutoff

The date the model's training data stops. It knows nothing about events, prices, releases, or news after that point, and often isn't sure exactly where its own cutoff is. Ask about last week and it may confidently answer from an outdated world.
Confidence is not a signal
The model sounds equally sure whether it's right, hallucinating, or answering from stale knowledge. You cannot tell from the tone, which is precisely why tone can't be your safety check.
It's worst on the specific and the obscure

Hallucination is most likely on precise, verifiable details (names, numbers, quotes, links, citations) about niche or recent topics, exactly the things that look most authoritative and are most tempting to copy.
Grounding reduces it

When you give the model the real source to work from, paste the document, or use a tool that searches, it has actual material to draw on instead of guessing. "Answer only from this text" is far safer than "answer from memory."
mistakes: Trusting a confident answer on a recent topic, the model's knowledge stops at its cutoff and it won't reliably tell you it's out of date
Copying specific details (quotes, statistics, citations, links) without checking, these are exactly what hallucination produces most convincingly
Believing the model when it 'cites a source', it can invent realistic-looking sources that don't exist
Assuming a newer or bigger model never hallucinates, better models hallucinate less, but none are immune
Asking it about today's news or live data and taking the answer at face value, without a search tool it literally cannot know
flags: "It gave me a source/quote/statistic", verify it exists before using it; fabricated-but-realistic references are a classic hallucination
"It told me about a recent event confidently", check whether that's even after its knowledge cutoff; it may be guessing from an old world
"It contradicted itself between answers", a sign it was generating plausible text rather than drawing on a stable fact
"It insisted it was right when I pushed back", confidence under pressure still isn't evidence; go check an actual source
ask: Is this about something recent? If so, is it past the model's knowledge cutoff, and do I need a search tool or a real source instead?
Would being wrong here actually cost me, and if so, how will I verify it independently?
Did the model give me specific, copyable details (numbers, names, quotes, links)? Those are the ones to check first.
Could I make this safer by giving the model the real source to answer from, instead of asking it from memory?

MODULES.title: Beyond Text
MODULES.tag: Images, files, the internet, and tools, the extras bolted onto the text engine
MODULES.why: By now you know the core model only predicts text, and only knows what's in its training and your prompt. So how can ChatGPT look at a photo, read your PDF, search the web, or run a calculation? The answer is that modern AI products bundle extra abilities around the text engine. Knowing which abilities are core to the model and which are bolt-on features explains what your particular tool can and can't do, and stops you from assuming every AI can do everything you've seen somewhere.
MODULES.mental: Think of the language model as a powerful engine, and the product you actually use (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) as a car built around that engine. The engine does text prediction. Everything else, seeing images, reading files, searching the internet, doing math, running code, is a capability the car adds on. Crucially, when the model needs something outside its own abilities, it doesn't magically gain a new power, it calls a tool: a separate piece of software that does the real work and hands the result back as text the model can use. So "can this AI do X?" almost always means "does this product give the model a tool for X?" Same engine, different cars, different features.
concepts: Multimodal (seeing and hearing)

Some models can take in more than text, an image, a screenshot, sometimes audio, and describe or reason about it. This is a real capability of those specific models, not every model has it, and the model is still predicting text, just text about what it was shown.
Reading files

When you attach a PDF or document, the product extracts the text and slips it into the prompt for you. The model isn't 'opening' the file, it's reading text the tool pulled out, which is why a scanned image with no real text can stump it.
Web search / browsing

By itself the model can't reach the internet. A search tool, when the product includes one, looks things up live and feeds the results into the prompt. That's how an AI can answer about today, it's reading fresh text the tool fetched, not 'knowing' it.
Tools (the general idea)

A tool is any outside helper the model can call: a calculator, a search engine, a code runner, a database. The model decides it needs help, the tool does the exact work, and the result comes back as text. This is how AI gets reliable at things text-prediction is bad at.
Why tools make it more reliable

Letting a calculator do the math, or a search engine fetch the fact, replaces a shaky guess with an actual answer. Tools are how products patch over the model's weak spots, arithmetic, fresh info, exact lookups, without changing the engine itself.
Generating images is a different model

When an AI 'draws' a picture, that's usually a separate image-generation model, not the text engine. The product routes your request to it. It's another example of capabilities bundled into one friendly interface.
mistakes: Assuming every AI can see images or search the web, those are features of specific products and models, not universal powers
Thinking the model 'opened' your file, the tool extracted the text first; a scanned or image-only PDF may have no text to read
Believing an answer is current just because the tool can search, check whether search actually ran for that answer, or whether it fell back on old training
Expecting the text model to do flawless math on its own, reliable arithmetic comes from a calculator tool, not the prediction engine
Confusing 'the AI generated an image' with the chat model drawing, that's usually a separate image model the product called
flags: "It couldn't read my PDF", it may be a scanned image with no extractable text, or the file was too long for the window
"It gave outdated info even though it can browse", search may not have run that turn; ask it explicitly to search, or check for a source link
"It got the math wrong", the plain text model was guessing; use a tool/calculator feature, or have it show and you verify the steps
"This works in one AI app but not another", different products bundle different tools; the capability isn't part of every model
ask: Does the tool I'm using actually have this capability (image input, web search, file reading), or am I assuming it from something I saw elsewhere?
For a fresh-info answer, did it really search, is there a source or link, or might it be answering from old training?
For anything exact (math, data lookup), is a tool doing the work, or is the model just predicting a plausible number?
Could giving it the source directly (paste the text, attach the file) be more reliable than hoping a tool fetched the right thing?

MODULES.title: Putting It Together
MODULES.tag: Choosing a model, building cost intuition, and where to go next
MODULES.why: You now know what the engine is, how it reads, what it forgets, how to talk to it, where it fails, and what the extras do. This final lesson ties it into practical judgment: how to pick a model for a task, a rough feel for what things cost, and a simple habit for deciding when to trust an answer. It's also your on-ramp, when you're ready to actually build things with these models, the Engineering Mastery course picks up right where this leaves off.
MODULES.mental: Everything in this course collapses into one working habit: match the model and your effort to what the task actually needs. A throwaway brainstorm doesn't need the biggest, priciest model or careful fact-checking. A client-facing claim or a medical question needs your best model, a tight prompt, real sources, and a human check. So before each task, ask two quick questions: how capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me? Cheap-and-fast for low stakes, careful-and-verified for high stakes. You're not memorizing rules, you're learning to right-size your tool, which is exactly how a professional uses one.
concepts: Bigger model vs smaller model

Most providers offer a range: larger, smarter, slower, pricier models, and smaller, faster, cheaper ones. The big one isn't always the right call. For simple tasks the small one is quicker and far cheaper; save the heavyweight for genuinely hard work.
A rough feel for cost

Cost tracks tokens, both what you send and what comes back. Short chats are nearly free; the expense comes from big pasted documents and long generated answers. You don't need exact numbers, just the instinct that 'huge input plus long output equals real money.'
Match effort to stakes

Low-stakes, reversible task? Move fast, accept a good-enough answer. High-stakes or hard-to-undo? Use a stronger model, give it sources, and verify the output yourself. Right-sizing your caution is the core skill.
Know when to verify

Trust the model for drafting, brainstorming, explaining, and rephrasing. Verify it for facts, numbers, recent events, citations, and anything where being wrong has a cost. This single split prevents most AI mishaps.
Pick the tool with the right features

If you need current info, choose a product with web search. If you work with images or PDFs, choose one that handles them. The 'best' AI is the one whose bundled capabilities match what you're actually doing.
The app is doing a lot for you

Every time you chat, the product is quietly working on your behalf: re-sending the whole conversation, slipping in a hidden system message, and routing your words to a model someone else chose. Builders do all of that themselves by calling the model directly through an API, a way for their own software to hand text to the model and get text back. You don't need to write a line of code to finish here, but seeing the chat app as a convenient wrapper around a raw model call is exactly the shift the Engineering Mastery course starts from.
Where to go next

If you want to go from using these models to building with them, designing prompts at scale, wiring up tools, controlling cost in real systems, that's the Engineering Mastery course. Everything here is the foundation it assumes.
mistakes: Always reaching for the biggest model, it's slower and costlier, and overkill for most everyday tasks
Ignoring cost until a surprise bill, a quick instinct about input and output size prevents nearly all of them
Applying the same caution to everything, a brainstorm and a legal question don't deserve the same scrutiny, or the same trust
Choosing an AI tool by hype rather than by whether it has the features your task needs (search, files, images)
Treating the model as either magic or useless, the skill is knowing which tasks it's great at and which need a check
flags: "This is taking forever and costing a lot", you may be on the heavyweight model for a simple task, or sending huge inputs; right-size both
"I'm not sure whether to trust this answer", run the split: drafting/brainstorming is fine; facts/numbers/recent/citations need verifying
"My tool can't do something I need", it may lack that feature; pick a product whose bundled capabilities fit the task
"I want to actually build with this, not just chat", that's the on-ramp to the Engineering Mastery course, this was the foundation
ask: How capable does the model really need to be for this, could a smaller, cheaper, faster one do just fine?
Roughly how many tokens is this, am I pasting a lot in or asking for a very long answer, and do I need to?
What are the stakes if this is wrong, and does that mean I should verify it or give it a real source?
Does my tool actually have the features this task needs, and if I'm ready to build, am I ready for the next course?

PLAIN.whatai: AI tools like ChatGPT are powered by something called a large language model. Underneath, it does one surprisingly simple thing: it predicts the next bit of text, again and again, until it has written a whole answer. It isn't looking things up, it has no real memory of you, and it doesn't "know" facts the way a person or a database does, it produces text that sounds right based on patterns it learned. That's why it can be incredibly helpful and also, sometimes, confidently wrong. This lesson is about that one core idea, because everything else in AI makes sense once you've got it.
PLAIN.tokens: Before an AI model can do anything with your text, it chops it into little pieces called tokens. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word, so common words are one piece and longer or unusual words get split into several. The model never sees letters or whole words the way you do, it sees this stream of tokens. That one fact quietly explains a lot: you're charged by the token (both what you type and what it writes back), length limits are counted in tokens, and the model's odd weak spots, like miscounting the letters in a word, happen because it isn't looking at letters at all. You won't count tokens by hand, but knowing they exist makes AI's cost and quirks stop being mysterious.
PLAIN.context: An AI model has no memory of its own. Every time you send a message, it's handed one big block of text, the conversation so far plus your new message, and it can only look at what fits in that block. The size of that block is called the context window, and it's the model's short-term memory, like a desk with a hard edge. Whatever's on the desk, it can use; whatever falls off the edge when the conversation gets too long is simply gone. That's why a model can 'forget' something you said much earlier, why pasting in a giant document can backfire, and why long chats slowly drift. The practical takeaway: you control what goes on the desk, and keeping it focused on what matters is the most useful AI skill there is.
PLAIN.prompting: A prompt is just the text you give an AI to work with, your question or instruction plus any context you include. The model takes it literally and can't read your mind, so the quality of your prompt drives the quality of the answer. The trick isn't secret phrases, it's treating the model like a brilliant new assistant on their first day: tell it clearly what you want done, give it the background it needs, and say what a good answer looks like (a list, a short paragraph, a friendly tone, a certain length). If the first reply is close but not quite right, just tell it what to change, prompting is a back-and-forth, not a one-shot spell. Vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out. This is the single highest-leverage skill in the whole course.
PLAIN.chat: Chatting with an AI feels like talking to someone who remembers the conversation, but the model itself remembers nothing between messages, it's what engineers call stateless. The continuity is an illusion created by the chat app: every time you hit send, the app re-sends the entire conversation so far, your messages and the model's replies, all glued together, plus your new message. The model reads that whole transcript, answers, and forgets again. That's why a brand-new chat starts blank (empty transcript), why 'memory' features are a separate add-on that saves notes and slips them into the transcript, and why a hidden 'system message' the product adds at the top can quietly shape every answer. Once you see that the memory lives in the re-sent transcript and not in the model, chat tools stop being mysterious.
PLAIN.limits: Models go wrong in two big, predictable ways, and both come from the same fact: the model predicts plausible-sounding text, it doesn't look things up. First, when it doesn't actually know something, it tends to make up a convincing answer rather than admit it, fake statistics, invented quotes, citations to papers that don't exist. That's called hallucination, and there's no setting that fully turns it off. Second, the model was trained once in the past, so its knowledge stops at a certain date, the knowledge cutoff, and it knows nothing newer unless a tool feeds it fresh information. Picture a brilliant expert locked in a room since last year who'd rather smoothly invent an answer than say 'I don't know.' The danger is that it sounds just as confident when it's wrong, so confidence is never your safety check. Be especially careful with specific details and anything recent, and verify anything where being wrong would cost you.
PLAIN.tools: The core AI model only predicts text, so how can your app look at a photo, read your PDF, search the web, or do math? Modern AI products bundle extra abilities around the text engine. Think of the model as an engine and the product (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) as a car built around it: seeing images, reading files, searching the internet, running calculations, these are features the car adds. When the model needs something outside its own ability, it calls a tool, a separate piece of software that does the real work and hands the result back as text. Reading a file means the tool pulled the text out; searching the web means a tool fetched fresh pages; getting the math right means a calculator did it. So 'can this AI do X?' really means 'does this product give the model a tool for X?' Same engine, different cars, different features, which is why two AI apps can have very different abilities.
PLAIN.using: This lesson ties everything together into a single working habit: match the model, and your own effort, to what the task actually needs. Providers offer bigger, smarter, slower, pricier models and smaller, faster, cheaper ones, and the big one isn't always right, save it for genuinely hard work. Cost tracks tokens, so short chats are nearly free and the expense comes from big pasted documents and long answers; you just need the instinct that 'huge input plus long output equals real money.' Before each task, ask two questions: how capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me? Move fast and accept good-enough for low-stakes work; use a stronger model, give it real sources, and verify the output for anything high-stakes. Trust it for drafting, brainstorming, and rephrasing; verify it for facts, numbers, recent events, and citations. That's how a professional uses the tool, and if you're ready to go from using these models to building with them, the Engineering Mastery course picks up right here.

GLOSSARY: A broad term for software that does things we used to think required human intelligence, like understanding language or recognizing images. Today, most of the "AI" people talk about is built on large language models.

The engine behind tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. A program trained on a huge amount of text whose core skill is predicting the next word, which turns out to be enough to write, answer, and reason.
Short for the AI program itself, the trained "brain" you send text to and get text back from. "The model" and "the LLM" usually mean the same thing.
The basic move an LLM makes: given the text so far, guess the most likely next chunk. Repeat that thousands of times and you get a full answer.
The one-time process of showing a model enormous amounts of text so it gets good at predicting it. Using the model afterward doesn't add to its training.
To produce new text on the spot, rather than look it up. LLMs generate answers, which is why they can be both creative and occasionally wrong.
Popular chat products, each built on top of a large language model. The differences you notice are mostly in the product wrapped around the model, not a different kind of engine.
The small chunk of text a model actually reads and writes, often a common word, a word-piece, or a punctuation mark. As a rough rule, one token is about four characters, or three-quarters of a word.
Slicing your text into tokens before the model sees it. It happens automatically every time, for both your input and the model's output.
Input tokens are everything you send in (your prompt plus any pasted text); output tokens are everything the model writes back. Both are counted, and both affect speed and cost.
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, a model can look at in one go. It must hold the whole conversation, your message, any pasted files, and the answer being written, all at once.
A plain-English name for what's in the context window right now: the only thing the model can actually use this turn. It doesn't remember anything outside that window by default.
What happens when a conversation grows past the window: the earliest messages stop being included, so the model can no longer refer to them, it's not choosing to forget, it simply can't see them.
The text you give the model to work with: your question or instruction plus any context or examples. It's the entire input the model has, so anything you leave out, it doesn't know.
The skill of writing clear instructions for a model. Less about clever tricks, more about saying plainly what you want, giving the needed context, and describing what a good answer looks like.

Refining your request after seeing the first answer, telling the model what to change ('shorter', 'more formal', 'focus on this') instead of rewriting from scratch. Prompting is a back-and-forth, not one shot.
Describes the model keeping no memory between turns: each message is handled on its own, as if it were the first. Any sense of an ongoing conversation comes from outside the model.
The running transcript of everything said so far, your messages and the model's replies. The chat app stores it and re-sends the whole thing each turn so the model has the full picture.

A hidden instruction most chat tools add at the very top of the transcript, before your first word, telling the model how to behave. You don't see it, but it shapes the tone and rules of every answer.

An optional extra, built on top of the model, that saves notes about you and slips them into the transcript automatically. The model didn't 'learn', the app just stores and re-inserts the notes; you can usually view and edit them.

When a model states something false as if it were true, a fake quote, an invented statistic, a citation to a paper that doesn't exist. It happens because the model fills gaps with plausible text instead of admitting it doesn't know.

The date a model's training data stops. It knows nothing about events, prices, or releases after that point, and often isn't sure exactly when its own cutoff is, so it may answer recent questions from an outdated world.
Giving the model real material to answer from, a pasted document or a tool's search results, instead of asking it from memory. Grounded answers are far less likely to be made up.

Describes a model that can take in more than text, such as images or audio, and reason about it. It's a capability of specific models, not a universal power, and the model is still producing text about what it was shown.

Any outside helper a model can call when it needs something beyond text prediction: a calculator, a web search, a code runner, a database. The tool does the real work and hands the result back as text the model can use.

A tool that lets an AI product look things up live on the internet and feed the results into the prompt. The core model can't reach the web by itself; this is a bolted-on feature, and not every product has it.

whatai.worked: Ask a model, "What's the capital of France?" and it answers "Paris", instantly and correctly. It feels like it looked that up in a database. It didn't. The phrase "the capital of France is" appeared so many times in its training text, always followed by "Paris", that "Paris" is overwhelmingly the most likely next word. The model is just completing the pattern. Now ask it, "What did I have for breakfast last Tuesday?" It has no way to know, but its job is to produce likely-sounding text, so it may cheerfully invent a plausible breakfast. Same engine, same behavior, completing text. The difference is that one pattern was all over its training data and the other one it had to make up. Holding both examples in your head at once is the whole lesson: right answers and made-up answers come out of the exact same machine, the same way.
good: You treat the model as a confident draft-writer, not a source of truth
You double-check anything where being wrong would actually cost you
You're not surprised when it makes something up, you expect it and verify
You reach for a real search or a document when you need current or private facts
You ask it to generate, brainstorm, rephrase, and explain, where it genuinely shines
whatai.build: Try this five-minute experiment in any chat AI. First, ask it a well-known fact ("What year did the first iPhone come out?"), it will likely nail it. Then ask it something it can't possibly know but that sounds answerable ("What's the name of the small café two doors down from my office?"). Watch it produce a confident, specific, and completely invented answer. Seeing the same tool be reliably right and confidently wrong, back to back, makes the "text-prediction machine" idea stick far better than any explanation.

tokens.worked: Take the simple sentence "I love tokenization!" To you, that's three words. To the model, it might be six or seven tokens: "I", " love" (the space rides along), " token", "ization", and "!". Notice three things. First, the common word "love" is a single token, but the longer, less common word "tokenization" got split into pieces. Second, spaces and punctuation are tokens too. Third, and this is the punchline, the model never saw the letters t-o-k-e-n; it saw the chunks " token" and "ization". So if you ask it, "how many letter z's are in that sentence?", it has to reason about something it can't actually see, and it often gets it wrong. The same blindness that makes it stumble on counting letters is exactly why it can read almost any text, in any language, including words it was never trained on: it just spells the unfamiliar word out of smaller, familiar tokens.
good: You think in rough tokens, not exact words, when you estimate length or cost (a chunky paragraph is a few hundred tokens, not a precise figure)
You remember that pasted text counts as input tokens, so you trim documents down to the part that matters
You don't ask the model to do letter-level tasks (counting characters, exact anagrams) and trust the result, you reach for a real tool
You're not surprised that a long answer costs more than a short one, output tokens are billed too
You notice that the same content can cost more in some languages, and factor that in if it matters

Finally, paste the same sentence translated into another language and compare the token count. In five minutes you'll have seen, with your own eyes, why common words are cheap, rare words are expensive, and the model reads in chunks rather than letters.

context.worked: Imagine a long chat with an assistant. Near the start, you mention, "My dog's name is Pixel." You then talk for forty more messages about a totally different project. Finally you ask, "What's my dog's name?" and the model says it doesn't know, or worse, confidently guesses "Max." It didn't betray you. As the conversation grew, it eventually got longer than the context window, and the earliest messages, including the one about Pixel, slid off the edge. From the model's point of view in that final turn, you simply never mentioned a dog. The model isn't remembering and then forgetting; each turn it only ever sees what currently fits in the window. Now flip it around: if instead you'd said, "Earlier I told you my dog's name, remind me to use it, his name is Pixel," right before asking, the detail would be back on the desk and the model would nail it. Same model, same question, completely different result, because of what was in the window at the moment you asked.
good: You restate key details when a conversation has gotten long, rather than assuming the model still has them
You paste in only the relevant part of a document, not the whole thing, so the important bit isn't buried
You start a fresh chat (with a short summary) when an old one has drifted, instead of fighting the drift
You keep one task per conversation when accuracy matters, so unrelated context doesn't confuse things
You put your actual question where it's easy to find, not buried under a wall of pasted text

Now ask, "What's my favorite number?" See whether it still has it. Part two: do it again, but this time restate the fact right before you ask. Watching the model lose a detail and then reliably keep it, just by changing what's in the window, turns 'the context window' from an abstract phrase into something you can feel.

prompting.worked: Watch one prompt improve in three steps. Step one, the vague version: "Write about our coffee shop." The model has nothing to go on, so it produces something generic that could describe any cafe anywhere. Step two, add the task and audience: "Write a short, warm welcome blurb for the About page of our neighborhood coffee shop, aimed at first-time visitors." Already far better, it now knows what, for whom, and the tone. Step three, add the shape and a detail: "...in three sentences, friendly but not cutesy, and mention that we roast our own beans." Now you'll get something you could almost paste straight in. Nothing clever happened, no magic words, you just told a capable assistant what you actually wanted. And if the result is still a touch off, you don't start over: you say "good, but make the first sentence punchier." That last move, refining instead of rewriting, is the habit that makes prompting feel easy.
good: You state the task plainly, what you want done, not just the topic
You include the context the model couldn't otherwise know (audience, goal, relevant background)
You say what a good answer looks like, format, length, and tone
You paste an example when you have one, and say 'like this'
You refine in small steps when the first answer is close, instead of starting from scratch
prompting.build: Pick any real task you'd actually use AI for, an email, a summary, a list of ideas. Write the laziest one-line prompt for it and note the answer. Then rewrite the prompt with three additions: the specific task, the context (who it's for, what it's about), and the format you want. Send it again and compare. Finally, take that second answer and refine it once with a single instruction ('shorter', 'warmer', 'add a call to action'). In five minutes you'll have felt the whole arc, vague to specific to refined, on a task you care about, which is the fastest way to make prompting a habit instead of a theory.

chat.worked: Here's the illusion taken apart. You open a chat and type "My name is Sam." The model replies, "Nice to meet you, Sam." Next you ask, "What's my name?" and it says "Sam." It feels like it remembered. But watch what the app actually sent on that second turn: not just "What's my name?", but the entire transcript, "My name is Sam." / "Nice to meet you, Sam." / "What's my name?", all glued together and handed over fresh. The model read the whole thing top to bottom and saw your name sitting right there in the text. It didn't recall anything; it re-read a transcript that happened to contain the answer. Now picture the same setup but a thousand messages long, until that first "My name is Sam" finally falls out of the context window. Ask "What's my name?" again and the model can't tell you, the line is no longer in the transcript it receives. Same model, same question, different answer, entirely because of what's in the re-sent transcript. The memory was never in the model; it was in the text being re-handed to it each turn.
good: You treat each new chat as a blank slate and bring in any detail you need from before
You understand the 'memory' is the re-sent transcript, not the model recalling anything
You restate key facts in a long chat rather than assuming earlier messages survived
When you turn on a memory feature, you check what it actually stored about you
You're not thrown when a hidden system message gives the tool a certain personality or rules

Part one: tell it a fact in a fresh chat ('I'm planning a trip to Lisbon'), then ask a couple of follow-ups, and watch it carry the detail, that's the transcript at work. Seeing it 'remember' in one window and draw a total blank in another, with no setting changed, makes statelessness click: the continuity lived in the conversation, not in the model.

limits.worked: Ask a model, "Give me three peer-reviewed studies showing that houseplants improve office productivity, with authors and years." You'll likely get exactly that: three crisp citations, real-sounding author names, plausible journals, recent years. It looks authoritative. Now try to find one of them, search the title, the authors. There's a good chance one or more simply does not exist. The model wasn't lying or broken; you asked for the shape of an answer (citations) on a specific topic, and it produced the most likely-looking text of that shape, inventing the details it didn't actually have. That's hallucination in its most dangerous form, because the polish makes it feel trustworthy. Now stack the second failure on top: ask it, "What major news happened last week?" and it may answer confidently about events, except its training stopped months or years ago, so it's describing a world that's out of date, with no built-in way to tell you so. One engine, two predictable failures, made-up specifics and stale knowledge, both wearing the same confident voice. Spotting them is the whole skill.
good: You verify specific, copyable details (quotes, numbers, citations, links) before relying on them
You check whether a question is about something recent, past the model's cutoff, and reach for search or a real source if so
You never use the model's confidence as a signal of correctness
You ground important questions by pasting the real source and saying 'answer only from this'
You stay a little skeptical exactly when an answer is most specific and most tempting to copy

Then actually try to verify one or two by searching. Notice how convincing the fabrications look. Next, ask it something clearly recent ('what's the latest version of X', 'what happened this month') and see whether it admits uncertainty or answers confidently from old knowledge. Doing this once, on purpose, in a low-stakes way, builds the instinct that protects you everywhere else: confident is not the same as correct.

tools.worked: Picture asking an AI, "What's 4,817 times 9,231, and what's the weather in Lisbon right now?" A plain text model, on its own, would guess at the multiplication (often landing close but wrong) and would have no idea about today's weather, its knowledge is frozen and it can't see outside. But in a modern product, something smarter happens. For the math, the model recognizes it needs help and calls a calculator tool: the calculator does the exact arithmetic and hands back the real number, which the model drops into its answer. For the weather, it calls a search tool that fetches the current conditions and feeds that fresh text into the prompt, now the model can report it accurately. Notice what changed: the engine didn't suddenly get good at math or gain a window to the world. The product routed each sub-task to a tool built for it, and the model stitched the results into one fluent reply. That's the entire pattern behind 'AI that can do anything', it's a text engine surrounded by helpers it knows how to call.
good: You know which abilities are core (text) and which are bolt-on tools (search, files, images, math)
You check whether your specific product actually has the capability you need
For fresh-info answers, you look for a sign that search really ran (a source or link)
You let a tool handle exact work (math, lookups) rather than trusting the model to guess it
You give the model the source directly when you can, instead of hoping a tool fetched the right thing

Ask it a tricky multiplication and check the result. In a few minutes you'll have mapped your specific tool's real capabilities, and you'll stop assuming every AI can do everything you've seen somewhere.

using.worked: Let's run two real tasks through the habit and watch the right choice fall out. Task one: brainstorm ten playful names for a houseplant shop. Stakes are low, it's reversible, and it's pure creative generation, the model's home turf. So: reach for a smaller, faster, cheaper model, write a quick prompt, and happily accept a good-enough list. No fact-checking needed, no heavyweight model, no fuss. Task two: draft a paragraph for a patient handout about a medication's side effects. Completely different. Being wrong here could hurt someone, so the stakes are high and the facts must be exact. Same person, same tool, two opposite approaches, and the deciding questions were just 'how capable does this need to be?' and 'what does being wrong cost me?' That's the whole course, distilled into a habit you can run in five seconds before any task.

whatai.mech:
Here's a little more of what's happening under the hood, no math required. When you send the model text, it first chops it into small chunks (you'll meet these as tokens in the next lesson). Then it runs those chunks through a giant web of numbers, learned during training, that has effectively absorbed the statistical patterns of how language tends to flow. The output of all that is a ranked list of likely next chunks, with a probability on each. The model picks one, adds it to the text, and runs the whole process again for the next chunk. It repeats this until it decides the answer is complete.

Two things follow from this, and they explain almost everything beginners find confusing. First, the model has no separate store of facts to check against. "Knowing" that Paris is the capital of France just means that, given the surrounding words, "Paris" comes out on top. When a fact was rare or absent in training, the most likely next words can be plausible-sounding nonsense, that's a hallucination, and it isn't a bug that gets patched away. Second, the model is frozen. Training happened once, in the past, so it has a knowledge cutoff and knows nothing about you or about events after that date, unless a product feature explicitly feeds it that information at the moment you ask.
trade: The same skill that lets it write and brainstorm freely is what lets it confidently make facts up
Fluency is the model's whole goal; it is not a signal that the answer is right
By itself the model can't know today's news or your private data; that needs an extra step, like search or pasting it in
scale: Helpful framing for everyday use, not engineering, since this is a foundations course: the bigger and more capable the model, the slower and more expensive each answer tends to be, so you don't need the biggest model for simple tasks
The same question can cost more or less depending on how long your input and the answer are, you'll see exactly why in the next lesson on tokens
If a tool feels slow, it's often the model writing a long answer one chunk at a time, asking for a shorter answer genuinely makes it faster

whatai.interview: Here's how I'd explain it to a friend in two sentences. A large language model is a text-prediction machine: you give it words, and it keeps guessing the most likely next word until it has written a full answer, like an incredibly well-read autocomplete. It isn't looking anything up and it doesn't truly know facts, which is why it can be amazingly helpful and also, sometimes, confidently and completely wrong.

tokens.mech:
A little more under the hood, still no math. Every model ships with a fixed vocabulary of tokens, often around fifty to a hundred thousand of them, built once when the model was made. The pieces aren't chosen by hand; a process scans huge amounts of text and keeps the chunks that show up most often. Very common words earn their own single token. Rarer words get assembled from smaller pieces, and truly unusual strings (a random password, a long chemical name) can break down almost letter by letter. That's the trade that makes the whole thing work: a manageable, fixed set of pieces that can still spell out absolutely anything.

This is why the model's view of text is genuinely different from yours, and it explains the quirks. It sees " token" + "ization", not t-o-k-e-n-i-z-a-t-i-o-n, so counting letters, reversing a word, or perfect spelling are awkward, the raw letters aren't really visible to it. It also explains cost and limits: since everything is measured in tokens, your bill and your length limit both track token counts, and languages that happen to split into more tokens cost more to process for the very same meaning. None of this is a flaw to be fixed; it's just the shape of how the model reads.
trade: Everyday words are cheap and quick; long, rare, or made-up words cost more tokens and a bit more processing
Lets it handle any text including unseen words, but makes letter-level tasks (counting, spelling, reversing) genuinely shaky
Fewer tokens is cheaper and faster; the skill is including what matters and trimming what doesn't
scale: Rough rule of thumb for everyday estimating: about seven hundred fifty words is around a thousand tokens, so a few pages of text is several thousand tokens
Both halves count toward cost: the text you send (input) and the text the model writes back (output), and the answer is often the bigger, pricier half
If a long answer feels slow, it's the model emitting tokens one at a time, asking for a shorter or more focused answer genuinely speeds things up and lowers cost
sec: Remember the text you paste is sent to the company running the model and counts as tokens, so don't paste secrets or other people's private data just to save yourself some typing
For any letter-perfect task (a license key, an exact code, a precise count of characters), don't trust the model's token's-eye view, double-check with a tool that actually sees the characters
If a vendor charges by tokens, a surprise bill usually traces back to large pasted inputs or very long outputs, watch both
tokens.interview: Here's the friend-explanation. Before an AI model reads your text, it chops it into little chunks called tokens, roughly three-quarters of a word each, so common words are one chunk and rare ones get split up. The model only ever sees those chunks, never the individual letters. That single fact explains three things at once: you're billed by the token for both what you type and what it writes, length limits are counted in tokens, and the model fumbles letter-level tasks like counting characters because it genuinely isn't looking at letters.

context.mech:
Here's what's really happening when you 'have a conversation' with an AI, and it surprises almost everyone. The model has no memory between turns. Each time you press send, the app quietly glues together the entire conversation so far, every earlier message from both of you, plus any files you attached and your new question, into one long block of text, and hands that whole block to the model fresh. The model reads it, predicts an answer, and then forgets it ever happened. The illusion of an ongoing chat is really the app re-sending the whole history every single time.

That block has a maximum size, the context window, measured in tokens. As long as the conversation fits, everything works and the model appears to 'remember.' But when the history grows past the window, something has to give: the app drops the oldest messages so the rest still fits. Those dropped messages are simply not in the block the model receives, so it cannot use them, it's not forgetting, it never saw them this turn. Two practical consequences follow. First, bigger windows help but never make the limit vanish, and a fuller window is slower and costs more. Second, more text is not automatically better: when the window is crammed with marginally-relevant stuff, the one detail that matters is easy to miss, which is why a focused context usually beats a giant one.
trade: Long chats drift as early context drops off; starting fresh with a short summary often restores accuracy
Paste everything vs paste the relevant part
A giant paste can bury the key detail and dilute the answer; a focused excerpt usually performs better
More room lets you include more, but every extra token in the window is slower and more expensive, and can add noise
scale: Context windows are advertised per model, often large enough for many pages and sometimes a whole book, but the limit is still real and still counted in tokens
A fuller window costs more and responds slower, because everything in it has to be processed every single turn, so don't fill it just because you can
If a chat is getting expensive or sluggish, it's often because the growing history is being re-sent each turn, summarizing and starting fresh resets that
sec: Everything in the window is something the model will read and may act on, so be careful pasting in text from untrusted sources, hidden instructions inside it can sway the answer
Don't leave sensitive details sitting in a long shared conversation longer than needed; what's in the window is what gets sent each turn
When precision matters, confirm the specific fact you care about is actually still in the conversation (not fallen off the edge) before you rely on the model's answer
context.interview: The friend-version goes like this. An AI model has no memory of its own, so every time you send a message, the app hands it the whole conversation so far plus your new message as one big block of text, and the model only sees what's in that block. The block has a size limit called the context window; when the chat grows past it, the oldest messages drop off and the model genuinely can't see them anymore. That's why it 'forgets' early details and why cramming in a huge document can backfire, the fix is to keep the window focused on what actually matters.

prompting.mech:
A little more on why phrasing matters so much, and it connects straight back to lesson one. The model predicts the next chunk of text based on everything in the prompt so far. Your prompt isn't a command that flips a switch; it's the starting text that steers every prediction that follows. A vague opening ("write about dogs") leaves the most-likely continuation wide open, so the model drifts toward the bland, average, could-be-anything answer, because that's statistically the safe path. A specific opening ("write a three-sentence, upbeat intro for a dog-walking flyer aimed at busy professionals") narrows the likely continuations dramatically, so the answer lands much closer to what you pictured.

This is also why examples are so powerful. When you paste a sample and say "like this," you've put a concrete pattern right into the text the model is continuing, and continuing a pattern is exactly what it's best at. And it's why iterating works: when you reply "shorter, and warmer," that feedback becomes part of the running prompt, so the next prediction is steered by it. You're not arguing with a person, you're adjusting the text that shapes the next guess. Seen this way, good prompting isn't a bag of tricks, it's just giving the prediction engine a clear, well-pointed starting line.
trade: A quick vague ask is less typing but gets a generic answer; a specific ask takes a moment longer and usually nails it
One big prompt vs step by step
Cramming every requirement in at once can lose one; breaking a complex task into steps is often more reliable
Describing the format works, but pasting one good example of it often teaches the model faster and more precisely
scale: A longer, more detailed prompt costs a few more tokens, this is almost always worth it, since a good answer the first time beats several cheap, useless ones
Iterating (a few short follow-ups) is cheap and fast, you don't have to get the perfect prompt on the first try, refining is a normal part of the flow
If you reuse a prompt often, it's worth polishing once and saving it; a good saved prompt pays for itself every time you use it
sec: Only include the context the task needs, don't paste private or sensitive details into a prompt just to be thorough, remember it's sent to the company running the model
Be specific about what you don't want too ("don't make up statistics," "only use the text I gave you"), it meaningfully reduces invented content
If an answer must be safe or accurate, say so in the prompt and still verify it, a good prompt lowers the odds of a bad answer but never guarantees one
prompting.interview: Here's the friend-explanation. A prompt is just the text you give the model, and it takes it completely literally, it can't read your mind or see your screen, so the clearer your instructions, the better the answer. Treat it like briefing a sharp new assistant on day one: say what you want done, give the context they'd need, and describe what a good result looks like, a list, a short paragraph, a friendly tone. And if the first reply is close but not quite right, you don't start over, you just tell it what to change. Prompting is a back-and-forth, not a magic phrase.

chat.mech:
Let's make the illusion fully concrete, because once you see it you can't unsee it. The model is a function that takes a block of text in and gives a block of text out, with nothing remembered in between. A chat app turns that memoryless function into a flowing conversation with one trick: it keeps a transcript. Every turn, it does the same four things, appends your new message to the transcript, glues the whole transcript into one text block (usually with a hidden system message pinned at the very top, setting the assistant's behavior), sends that entire block to the model, and appends the reply back onto the transcript. Repeat. The model never sees a 'conversation', it sees one long document, freshly handed over each turn.

Three real consequences fall out of this. First, a new chat is a new transcript, empty except for the system message, which is why it knows nothing about your other chats. Second, this is where the context window from lesson three bites: as the transcript grows past the window, the oldest lines get trimmed to fit, so 'it forgot' is really 'that line is no longer in the document it received.' Third, a memory feature is just an extra step that, before sending, looks up saved notes about you and quietly inserts them into the transcript, the model still didn't learn anything, the app just put the note in front of it. The whole magic of chat is bookkeeping around a function with no memory.
trade: A memoryless model is simpler and more predictable; the app re-sending the transcript is what creates the feeling of memory
No memory feature vs memory on
Off means every chat starts clean (more private, more repetitive); on means it recalls saved notes (handier, but stores things about you)
Long single chat vs fresh chats
One long chat keeps everything until it overflows the window; starting fresh keeps things clean but you re-supply what matters
scale: Because the whole transcript is re-sent every turn, a long conversation gets more expensive and slower with each message, it's not just your latest question being processed, it's everything before it too
Starting a fresh chat with a short summary resets that cost, you carry forward only what matters instead of dragging the entire history
Memory features and hidden system messages add a little to every prompt, usually small, but it's text that gets sent each turn alongside your own
sec: What's in the transcript is what gets sent each turn, so don't leave passwords or sensitive personal details sitting in a long conversation longer than you need them
If a memory feature is on, periodically check what it has saved about you, it's inserting those notes into your chats, and you can usually view, edit, or clear them
Be cautious pasting text from untrusted sources into a chat, hidden instructions buried in it become part of the transcript the model reads and may sway its replies
chat.interview: The friend-version: when you chat with an AI, it feels like it's remembering the conversation, but the model itself remembers nothing between messages, it's what's called stateless. The trick is that the chat app re-sends the entire conversation so far, every message from both of you, plus a hidden instruction at the top, as one big block of text every single turn. The model reads that whole transcript, replies, and forgets again. So the 'memory' isn't in the model, it's in the transcript the app keeps re-handing it, which is exactly why a brand-new chat starts blank.

limits.mech:
Both failures trace back to one line from lesson one: the model outputs the most likely next text, it has no separate store of facts to check against. So picture the model reaching a point where the honest answer is 'I don't actually know.' Nothing in the machinery produces that pause. It still has to emit the most plausible continuation, and a confident, specific-sounding answer is statistically more 'answer-shaped' than a hedge, so out comes a fluent fabrication. That's a hallucination: not a lie, not a bug, just the prediction engine doing its only job where it lacks real material. This is why it's worst on precise, obscure details, there the gap between 'sounds right' and 'is right' is widest, and why grounding (handing it the real source) helps so much: now the likely-next-text is anchored to actual material instead of thin air.

The knowledge cutoff is the second failure and it's even simpler. Training happened once, ending on some date. Everything after that, last week's news, this year's prices, the newest release, was never in the data, so the patterns simply aren't there. Worse, the model usually can't reliably report its own cutoff or notice that your question is about 'after' it, so it answers from its frozen worldview with the same confidence as everything else. Put the two together and you get the rule that protects you: be most careful exactly when an answer is most specific or most recent, because that's where confident and correct are most likely to come apart.
trade: The drive to always produce an answer is what makes it useful and what makes it hallucinate; it rarely just says 'I don't know'
By itself it's stuck at its cutoff; a search tool can fetch fresh info, but only if the product has one and it actually runs
Answer from memory vs from a source
Asking from memory is easy but guess-prone; pasting the real source ('use only this') trades a little effort for far fewer made-up facts
scale: Stronger, larger models tend to hallucinate less and have more recent cutoffs, but 'less' is not 'never', so the verify-the-important-stuff habit applies to every model
Grounding the model in a pasted source or a search result usually costs more tokens (you're sending more text), and it's almost always worth it when accuracy matters
Asking the model to show its reasoning or cite where a claim came from costs a little more output but makes it far easier for you to catch a fabrication
sec: Never let a model be the last word on anything safety-critical, medical, legal, financial, or where someone could be harmed, use it to get oriented, then confirm with a qualified human or an authoritative source
Treat any specific quote, statistic, citation, or link as unverified until you've checked it exists, realistic-looking fabricated references are the most common and most damaging hallucination
For recent or time-sensitive questions, assume the model may be out of date unless you can confirm a search tool actually ran and pulled current information
limits.interview: Here's how I'd put it to a friend. AI models fail in two predictable ways, and both come from the fact that they predict likely text instead of looking things up. First, when a model doesn't really know something, it tends to invent a convincing answer rather than admit it, fake quotes, made-up statistics, citations to papers that don't exist, that's called hallucination, and there's no setting that fully turns it off. Second, it was trained once in the past, so its knowledge stops at a cutoff date and it knows nothing newer. Picture a brilliant expert locked in a room since last year who'd rather smoothly make something up than say 'I don't know.' The catch is it sounds just as confident when it's wrong, so always double-check anything specific or recent.

tools.mech:
Here's the mechanism behind 'AI that can do anything', and it's tidier than it looks. The text model stays exactly what you learned: a next-text predictor that knows only its training and the current prompt. Tools are separate programs the product makes available, a calculator, a web search, a file reader, a code runner, an image generator. The clever part is that the model can be trained to recognize when a task is beyond it and to emit a little request like 'search for X' or 'calculate Y' instead of guessing.
